title: Your C binary file works on your laptop and breaks everywhere else
description:
A single fwrite call is the simplest way to save data in C -- and the fastest way to create a file that only your machine can read. This Short shows the two portability traps in raw binary dumps: byte order (endianness) and compiler-chosen struct padding, plus the fix (write field by field in a fixed byte order, with a magic number and version header).

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-2/05-binary-file-io/

#Shorts

beats.narration: You saved your app's data with one fwrite call. It loads perfectly on your laptop. On a coworker's machine, same file, same code, it comes back as garbage.
One reason: the integer one might be stored as a zero-one byte then zeros, or the exact reverse, depending on the CPU. The file's bytes never changed, but the value they decode to did.

There's also struct padding, which the compiler picks per platform, so your record's size can differ between builds. Safer: write each field in a fixed byte order, starting with a magic number and a version.
Raw struct dumps are fine for caches only your machine reads. Anything crossing machines, serialize field by field, or use JSON, CBOR, or Protocol Buffers.
Full breakdown, with the record database example, is in the lesson.
